title: Contract Formation
text:
A contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties. For a contract to be valid, several essential elements must be present. First, there must be an offer — a clear proposal by one party to another on specific terms. Second, there must be acceptance — an unconditional agreement to all the terms of the offer. Third, there must be consideration — something of value exchanged between the parties, such as money, goods, or services. Finally, both parties must have the legal capacity to enter into a contract.

When an offer is made, the offeree may respond in one of three ways: they may accept the offer, reject it outright, or make a counteroffer. A counteroffer is itself a new offer that rejects the original terms. If the offeree makes a counteroffer, the original offeror is under no obligation to accept it.

Contracts may be written or oral, though certain types — such as those involving the sale of land or agreements lasting more than one year — must be in writing to be enforceable under the Statute of Frauds.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of a valid contract?
questions.correct: Written form
questions.explanation: Most contracts do not need to be in writing. Written form is only required for specific types of contracts under the Statute of Frauds.

questions.question: When a counteroffer is made, what happens to the original offer?
questions.correct: It is rejected
questions.explanation: A counteroffer rejects the original offer entirely. The original offeror is no longer bound by the original offer.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is 'consideration'?
options: Something of value exchanged between parties
questions.correct: Something of value exchanged between parties
questions.explanation: Consideration is one of the essential elements of a valid contract — it refers to something of value (money, goods, services) given by each party.

questions.question: Under the Statute of Frauds, which type of contract must be in writing?
options: Contracts involving the sale of land
questions.correct: Contracts involving the sale of land
questions.explanation: The Statute of Frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing, including those for the sale of land and agreements lasting more than one year.

questions.question: What does 'offeree' mean in the context of this passage?
options: The person who makes the offer
The person who receives the offer
questions.correct: The person who receives the offer
questions.explanation: The offeree is the party to whom an offer is made. They may accept, reject, or make a counteroffer.

title: Breach of Contract and Remedies
text:
A breach of contract occurs when one party fails to perform their obligations under a valid contract without lawful excuse. Breaches can be classified as material or minor. A material breach is a fundamental failure that defeats the purpose of the contract, entitling the innocent party to treat the contract as terminated and to claim damages. A minor breach, by contrast, does not go to the root of the contract and only entitles the innocent party to claim damages.

When a breach occurs, the innocent party has several remedies available. Damages are the most common remedy — the court awards a sum of money to compensate the innocent party for their loss. Specific performance is an equitable remedy ordering the breaching party to actually carry out their contractual obligations. This remedy is typically granted where damages would be inadequate, such as in contracts for unique property.

The innocent party also has a duty to mitigate their loss. This means they must take reasonable steps to reduce the damage caused by the breach. Failure to mitigate may result in a reduction of the damages awarded.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a material and a minor breach?
options: A material breach involves a written contract; a minor breach is oral
A material breach defeats the purpose of the contract; a minor breach does not
A material breach always involves financial loss; a minor breach does not
A material breach requires proof of intent; a minor breach does not
questions.correct: A material breach defeats the purpose of the contract; a minor breach does not
questions.explanation: A material breach is fundamental — it goes to the root of the contract. A minor breach is less serious and only entitles the innocent party to damages, not termination.

questions.question: When is specific performance typically awarded?
options: When damages would be inadequate, such as for unique property
When both parties agree to it
questions.correct: When damages would be inadequate, such as for unique property
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy granted when money damages are insufficient — for example, where the subject matter is unique and cannot be replaced.

questions.question: What does the 'duty to mitigate' require?
options: The breaching party must pay double damages
The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce their loss
Both parties must agree to mediation
The court must approve all settlements
questions.correct: The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce their loss
questions.explanation: The duty to mitigate requires the innocent party to act reasonably to minimise their losses. Failure to do so can reduce the damages they receive.

questions.question: Which remedy does the court most commonly award for breach of contract?
questions.correct: Damages
questions.explanation: Damages — a monetary award to compensate for loss — is the primary remedy for breach of contract. Other remedies like specific performance are less common.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes 'specific performance'?
options: A financial penalty imposed by the court
A court order requiring a party to fulfil their contractual obligations
An agreement to terminate the contract
A form of compensation paid in instalments
questions.correct: A court order requiring a party to fulfil their contractual obligations
questions.explanation: Specific performance is a court order compelling the breaching party to actually perform what they promised under the contract.

collocations.sentence: The innocent party was entitled to ___ the contract as terminated after the material breach.
The court awarded ___ to compensate the claimant for the financial loss suffered.

title: Negligence in Tort Law
text:
Negligence is one of the most significant torts in English law. To establish a claim in negligence, the claimant must prove three elements: first, that the defendant owed them a duty of care; second, that the defendant breached that duty; and third, that the breach caused the claimant's loss or damage.

The duty of care was famously established in the case of Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), where the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owed a duty of care to the ultimate consumer of their product. Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' states that we owe a duty of care to those who are so closely and directly affected by our acts that we ought reasonably to have them in contemplation.

Once a duty of care is established, the claimant must show that the defendant fell below the standard of a 'reasonable person' in the circumstances. This is an objective test — the court asks what a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have done. If the defendant's conduct fell below this standard, they are said to have breached their duty.

Finally, the claimant must show that the breach caused the damage suffered. The basic test is the 'but for' test: but for the defendant's breach, would the claimant have suffered the loss?

questions.question: What are the three elements a claimant must prove in a negligence claim?
questions.correct: Duty of care, breach, causation
questions.explanation: To succeed in negligence, a claimant must prove: (1) the defendant owed a duty of care, (2) the defendant breached that duty, and (3) the breach caused the loss.

questions.question: What is the standard used to determine if a duty of care has been breached?
options: The standard of the defendant's profession
The standard of a reasonable person
The standard agreed in the contract
questions.correct: The standard of a reasonable person
questions.explanation: The test for breach is objective — the court asks whether a 'reasonable person' in the defendant's position would have acted differently.

questions.question: What is the 'but for' test used to determine?
options: Whether the defendant intended to cause harm
Whether the breach caused the claimant's loss
Whether the defendant owed a duty of care
questions.correct: Whether the breach caused the claimant's loss
questions.explanation: The 'but for' test asks: but for the defendant's negligent act, would the claimant have suffered the loss? If yes, causation is not established.

questions.question: In which case was the duty of care famously established?
options: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
questions.correct: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932)
questions.explanation: Donoghue v Stevenson is the landmark negligence case establishing that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the end consumer of their product.

questions.question: Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' refers to those to whom we owe a duty of care. Who are our 'neighbours' in legal terms?
options: People who are closely and directly affected by our acts
People we have a contract with
People who are related to us
questions.correct: People who are closely and directly affected by our acts
questions.explanation: Lord Atkin defined our 'neighbours' as those who are so closely and directly affected by our acts that we ought reasonably to have them in contemplation when we act.

collocations.sentence: The defendant ___ a duty of care to the claimant as the ultimate consumer of the product.
The surgeon fell ___ the standard of a reasonable medical professional.

title: Company Directors and Their Duties
text:
Directors occupy a pivotal role in the governance of a company. Under the Companies Act 2006, directors in England and Wales are subject to a comprehensive set of statutory duties. These duties are owed to the company itself, not to individual shareholders or third parties.

The primary duties include: the duty to act within the company's constitution and to exercise powers only for the purposes for which they were conferred; the duty to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole; the duty to exercise independent judgment; the duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence; and the duty to avoid conflicts of interest.

The duty to avoid conflicts of interest is particularly significant. A director must not allow personal interests to conflict with those of the company. If a director has a personal interest in a proposed transaction, they must declare that interest to the board. Failure to disclose a conflict of interest may render the transaction voidable and expose the director to personal liability.

Where a director breaches their duties, the company may seek various remedies, including damages, account of profits, or injunctive relief to prevent further breaches.

questions.question: To whom are a director's statutory duties owed?
questions.correct: To the company itself
questions.explanation: Under the Companies Act 2006, directors owe their duties to the company as a whole, not to individual shareholders or third parties.

questions.question: What must a director do if they have a personal interest in a proposed transaction?
options: Declare the interest to the board
questions.correct: Declare the interest to the board
questions.explanation: A director with a personal interest in a transaction must disclose it to the board. Failure to do so can make the transaction voidable and expose the director to liability.

questions.question: What is the consequence of a director failing to disclose a conflict of interest?
options: The transaction may be voidable and the director may face personal liability
The company must pay a fine
The shareholders must vote on the issue
questions.correct: The transaction may be voidable and the director may face personal liability
questions.explanation: Failure to disclose a conflict of interest may render the transaction voidable (capable of being set aside) and expose the director to personal liability for breach of duty.

questions.question: Which statute sets out directors' duties in England and Wales?
questions.correct: The Companies Act 2006
questions.explanation: Directors' statutory duties in England and Wales are set out in the Companies Act 2006, which consolidated and codified the common law duties.

questions.question: What remedy allows a company to claim profits made by a director who breached their duties?
questions.correct: Account of profits
questions.explanation: An account of profits is an equitable remedy requiring the director to hand over any profit they made as a result of their breach of duty.

collocations.sentence: The director must ___ a conflict of interest to the board before the transaction proceeds.

title: Employment Rights: Dismissal
text:
The law governing dismissal in England and Wales distinguishes between two main types: wrongful dismissal and unfair dismissal. These are distinct legal concepts with different requirements and remedies.

Wrongful dismissal is a common law claim arising from a breach of the employment contract. It typically occurs when an employer terminates an employee's contract without giving the correct period of notice, or in breach of a contractual term. The remedy for wrongful dismissal is damages equivalent to the notice pay the employee should have received.

Unfair dismissal, by contrast, is a statutory right under the Employment Rights Act 1996. To bring a claim for unfair dismissal, an employee must generally have been employed for at least two years. The employer must show that the dismissal was for a fair reason — such as conduct, capability, redundancy, or some other substantial reason — and that they followed a fair procedure. An employment tribunal may award compensation or, in some cases, reinstatement.

Redundancy is a potentially fair reason for dismissal. It arises where the employer's need for a particular role ceases or diminishes. Employers must follow a fair selection process and consider alternative employment within the organisation before making an employee redundant.

questions.question: What is the main difference between wrongful dismissal and unfair dismissal?
options: Wrongful dismissal is a statutory claim; unfair dismissal is a common law claim
Wrongful dismissal is a contract law claim; unfair dismissal is a statutory claim
Wrongful dismissal applies to all workers; unfair dismissal only applies to directors
They are the same thing described differently
questions.correct: Wrongful dismissal is a contract law claim; unfair dismissal is a statutory claim
questions.explanation: Wrongful dismissal is a common law (contract) claim for breach of the employment contract. Unfair dismissal is a statutory right under the Employment Rights Act 1996.

questions.question: How long must an employee typically have been employed to bring an unfair dismissal claim?
questions.correct: 2 years
questions.explanation: Under the Employment Rights Act 1996, employees generally need at least two years' continuous employment to bring an unfair dismissal claim.

questions.question: What is the remedy for wrongful dismissal?
options: Damages equivalent to the notice pay owed
A public apology from the employer
Compensation up to a statutory cap
questions.correct: Damages equivalent to the notice pay owed
questions.explanation: The remedy for wrongful dismissal is common law damages — typically the salary the employee would have earned during the correct notice period.

questions.question: Which of the following is a potentially fair reason for dismissal mentioned in the passage?
options: The employee made a protected disclosure
questions.correct: Redundancy
questions.explanation: Redundancy is explicitly listed in the Employment Rights Act 1996 as a potentially fair reason for dismissal, provided a fair process is followed.

questions.question: Before making an employee redundant, what must the employer consider?
options: Whether the employee has a mortgage
Whether the employee agrees to redundancy
questions.correct: Alternative employment within the organisation
questions.explanation: Before making an employee redundant, employers must consider whether there is suitable alternative employment within the organisation to offer the employee.

collocations.sentence: The employer must show that the dismissal was for a ___ reason.
The employee was awarded compensation by the employment ___.

title: Intellectual Property: Copyright and Infringement
text:
Copyright is a form of intellectual property that automatically protects original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works. Unlike patents or trademarks, copyright does not require registration — it arises automatically upon the creation of an original work. In the United Kingdom, copyright is governed primarily by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.

Copyright gives the owner the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, perform, display, or create derivative works from the original. These rights are limited in time: in general, copyright in a literary work lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 70 years after their death.

Copyright infringement occurs when someone exercises one of the copyright owner's exclusive rights without permission or a lawful defence. A common defence is fair dealing, which permits limited use of a copyrighted work for purposes such as research, private study, criticism, review, or news reporting, without requiring the copyright holder's consent.

Where infringement is established, the copyright owner may seek various remedies, including an injunction to prevent further infringement, damages to compensate for loss suffered, and an account of profits earned by the infringer.

questions.question: How is copyright different from patents and trademarks?
options: Copyright must be renewed every year
questions.correct: Copyright does not require registration
questions.explanation: Unlike patents and trademarks, copyright arises automatically upon creation of an original work — no registration is needed.

questions.question: How long does copyright in a literary work typically last in the UK?
questions.correct: The author's lifetime plus 70 years
questions.explanation: In the UK, copyright in literary works lasts for the lifetime of the author plus 70 years after their death.

questions.question: What is the 'fair dealing' defence?
options: A right to use any work freely for commercial purposes
A defence permitting limited use for purposes like research or criticism without consent
An agreement between the copyright owner and the user
A court order allowing publication of copyrighted material
questions.correct: A defence permitting limited use for purposes like research or criticism without consent
questions.explanation: Fair dealing allows limited use of copyrighted material for specific purposes (research, criticism, news reporting) without the copyright owner's permission.

questions.question: When does copyright infringement occur?
options: When someone admires a copyrighted work
When someone exercises the owner's exclusive rights without permission
When someone purchases a copyrighted work
When someone mentions a copyrighted work in conversation
questions.correct: When someone exercises the owner's exclusive rights without permission
questions.explanation: Copyright infringement occurs when someone exercises one of the exclusive rights — such as reproduction or distribution — without the owner's permission or a lawful defence.

questions.question: Which remedy prevents further copyright infringement?
questions.correct: Injunction
questions.explanation: An injunction is a court order that prohibits a party from continuing an infringing activity. It is used to prevent future infringement, not compensate for past harm.

collocations.sentence: Copyright ___ automatically upon the creation of an original work.

title: Arbitration and Dispute Resolution
text:
Arbitration has become an increasingly popular method of resolving commercial disputes, particularly in international business. Unlike litigation, which takes place in open court, arbitration is a private process in which the parties agree to submit their dispute to one or more independent arbitrators, whose decision — known as an award — is final and binding.

One of the key advantages of arbitration over litigation is confidentiality. Court proceedings are generally public, whereas arbitration hearings and awards are private, which is particularly attractive to commercial parties who wish to protect sensitive business information. Additionally, arbitration can be faster and more cost-effective than litigation in complex commercial disputes.

The foundation of arbitration is the arbitration agreement — a contractual clause providing that disputes will be resolved by arbitration rather than through the courts. Such clauses are given considerable weight by English courts, which will generally stay court proceedings where a valid arbitration agreement exists.

However, arbitration is not without its drawbacks. The right to appeal an arbitral award is very limited, and the costs of arbitration — particularly in international proceedings with three arbitrators — can be substantial. Furthermore, arbitration is not appropriate for all types of disputes; for example, matters involving insolvency or criminal law cannot generally be resolved through arbitration.

questions.question: What makes an arbitral award different from a court judgment?
options: An arbitral award can be appealed more easily
An arbitral award is not legally binding
An arbitral award is private and the right to appeal is very limited
An arbitral award requires government approval
questions.correct: An arbitral award is private and the right to appeal is very limited
questions.explanation: Unlike court judgments, arbitral awards are private (confidential) and the grounds for appeal are very narrow — generally limited to serious procedural irregularities.

questions.question: Why is confidentiality an advantage of arbitration for commercial parties?
options: It allows parties to avoid paying taxes
It protects sensitive business information from becoming public
It prevents the other party from knowing the outcome
It allows the arbitrator to decide without hearing both sides
questions.correct: It protects sensitive business information from becoming public
questions.explanation: Commercial parties often deal with sensitive business information. Unlike open court proceedings, arbitration hearings and awards are private, protecting this information.

questions.question: What is the 'arbitration agreement' referred to in the passage?
options: A court order to use arbitration
A contractual clause providing that disputes will be resolved by arbitration
An agreement signed after a dispute arises
A government regulation on dispute resolution
questions.correct: A contractual clause providing that disputes will be resolved by arbitration
questions.explanation: An arbitration agreement (or clause) is typically included in a contract, providing in advance that any disputes arising from the contract will be resolved through arbitration.

questions.question: According to the passage, which type of dispute CANNOT generally be resolved through arbitration?
questions.correct: Insolvency matters
questions.explanation: The passage states that matters involving insolvency or criminal law cannot generally be resolved through arbitration — these require court intervention.

questions.question: What will English courts generally do when a valid arbitration agreement exists?
options: Override the arbitration agreement and hear the case
Stay court proceedings and refer the parties to arbitration
Appoint a judge to act as arbitrator
questions.correct: Stay court proceedings and refer the parties to arbitration
questions.explanation: English courts give significant weight to arbitration agreements. If a valid agreement exists, courts will generally stay (pause) any court proceedings and require the parties to use arbitration.

collocations.sentence: The parties agreed to ___ their dispute to a panel of three arbitrators.
The arbitration clause gave the arbitrators ___ jurisdiction over all contractual disputes.
The court agreed to ___ the proceedings pending the outcome of the arbitration.

title: Insolvency and Liquidation
text:
Insolvency arises when a company or individual is unable to pay its debts as they fall due, or when its liabilities exceed its assets. In England and Wales, the insolvency of companies is primarily governed by the Insolvency Act 1986, which provides a range of procedures depending on the severity of the company's financial difficulties.

For companies facing temporary financial difficulties but with viable underlying businesses, administration may be appropriate. An administrator is appointed to manage the company's affairs with the objective of rescuing the company as a going concern, achieving a better result for creditors than immediate liquidation, or realising assets for the benefit of secured creditors.

Where rescue is not possible, the company may enter liquidation — also known as 'winding up'. In compulsory liquidation, a court order is made on the petition of a creditor or the company itself. In voluntary liquidation, the shareholders or creditors initiate the process without a court order. Upon liquidation, a liquidator is appointed to collect and sell the company's assets, pay creditors in a prescribed order of priority, and distribute any surplus to shareholders.

The order of priority in distributing assets is significant: secured creditors (those with a fixed or floating charge over the company's assets) are paid first, followed by preferential creditors (such as employees), then unsecured creditors, and finally shareholders. In practice, unsecured creditors and shareholders frequently receive little or nothing.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of administration?
options: To immediately sell the company's assets
To rescue the company as a going concern where possible
To prosecute the directors for misconduct
questions.correct: To rescue the company as a going concern where possible
questions.explanation: The primary objective of administration is to rescue the company as a going concern. Only if that is not possible does the administrator pursue other objectives such as better returns for creditors.

questions.question: What is the difference between compulsory and voluntary liquidation?
options: Compulsory liquidation is initiated by a court order; voluntary liquidation is initiated by shareholders or creditors
Compulsory liquidation is for individuals; voluntary liquidation is for companies
Compulsory liquidation is faster; voluntary liquidation is more expensive
There is no practical difference between the two
questions.correct: Compulsory liquidation is initiated by a court order; voluntary liquidation is initiated by shareholders or creditors
questions.explanation: Compulsory liquidation requires a court order (usually on a creditor's petition). Voluntary liquidation is initiated by the shareholders or creditors without court intervention.

questions.question: Who is paid FIRST in the distribution of assets on liquidation?
questions.correct: Secured creditors
questions.explanation: The order of priority gives secured creditors (those with charges over the company's assets) first claim on the proceeds of liquidation.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'going concern' mean in the context of insolvency?
options: A company that continues to operate as a functioning business
A company that is being investigated
A company in the process of being sold
questions.correct: A company that continues to operate as a functioning business
questions.explanation: A 'going concern' refers to a business that is operating normally and expected to continue doing so. Rescuing a company 'as a going concern' means keeping it operational rather than breaking it up.

questions.question: According to the passage, what typically happens to unsecured creditors in liquidation?
options: They are paid in full before shareholders
They frequently receive little or nothing
They are treated the same as secured creditors
They become shareholders in the new company
questions.correct: They frequently receive little or nothing
questions.explanation: Unsecured creditors rank below secured and preferential creditors in the order of priority. In practice, by the time higher-priority creditors are paid, little or nothing remains for unsecured creditors.

collocations.sentence: The company entered ___ after the court granted a winding-up order.
Secured creditors hold a charge ___ the company's assets.

title: Criminal Law: Mens Rea and Actus Reus
text:
In English criminal law, a person cannot generally be convicted of an offence unless the prosecution proves two fundamental elements beyond reasonable doubt: the actus reus (the guilty act) and the mens rea (the guilty mind). These Latin terms form the cornerstone of criminal liability.

The actus reus refers to the physical conduct element of a crime — the act, omission, or state of affairs that the law prohibits. It is important to note that criminal liability can arise not only from positive acts but also from omissions where the defendant was under a legal duty to act. For example, a parent who fails to provide medical care for a child may be criminally liable for that omission.

The mens rea refers to the mental element — the defendant's state of mind at the time of the offence. Different offences require different levels of mens rea. Intention (meaning the defendant desired the outcome or knew it was virtually certain to occur) represents the highest form of mens rea. Recklessness (where the defendant foresaw a risk but proceeded regardless) represents a lower degree of fault. Some offences require only negligence, or even impose strict liability, where no fault element is required at all.

Concurrence is also required — the actus reus and the mens rea must coincide at the same moment in time. Where the defendant's guilty act and guilty mind do not align, the defendant may escape criminal liability.

questions.question: What must the prosecution prove to convict a person of a criminal offence?
options: Both the actus reus and the mens rea beyond reasonable doubt
Either the actus reus or the mens rea
questions.correct: Both the actus reus and the mens rea beyond reasonable doubt
questions.explanation: Both elements must be proved beyond reasonable doubt: the actus reus (guilty act) and the mens rea (guilty mind). The absence of either element is a defence.

questions.question: Can criminal liability arise from an omission (failure to act)?
options: No, only positive acts can give rise to criminal liability
Yes, but only where the defendant was under a legal duty to act
Yes, any omission can give rise to criminal liability
No, omissions are always treated as civil matters
questions.correct: Yes, but only where the defendant was under a legal duty to act
questions.explanation: Criminal liability for omissions arises only where the defendant was under a legal duty to act — for example, a parent's duty to care for their child.

questions.question: What is the difference between intention and recklessness as forms of mens rea?
options: Intention requires proof; recklessness does not
Intention means desiring the outcome; recklessness means foreseeing a risk and proceeding anyway
Intention is always required; recklessness is only relevant for civil claims
They are the same thing described differently
questions.correct: Intention means desiring the outcome; recklessness means foreseeing a risk and proceeding anyway
questions.explanation: Intention (the highest form of mens rea) means the defendant desired the result. Recklessness means the defendant foresaw the risk but took it anyway — a lower level of fault.

questions.question: What is meant by 'concurrence' in criminal law?
options: The agreement of two or more defendants to commit a crime
The actus reus and mens rea must coincide at the same time
The prosecution and defence must agree on the facts
Two separate crimes committed by the same person
questions.correct: The actus reus and mens rea must coincide at the same time
questions.explanation: Concurrence requires that the guilty act and guilty mind must exist at the same moment. If they do not coincide, criminal liability may not arise.

questions.question: What is meant by 'strict liability' as mentioned in the passage?
options: A crime requiring the highest level of proof
An offence where no fault element (mens rea) is required
A civil claim rather than a criminal one
questions.correct: An offence where no fault element (mens rea) is required
questions.explanation: Strict liability offences do not require proof of any mental element — the prosecution only needs to prove the actus reus. These are typically regulatory offences.

collocations.sentence: The prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt ___ reasonable doubt.
The defendant was ___ a legal duty to act, which gave rise to liability for his omission.
The actus reus and mens rea must ___ at the same point in time.

title: Defamation: Libel and Slander
text:
Defamation is the publication of a false statement that tends to lower the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking members of society. English defamation law distinguishes between two forms: libel (permanent form, such as writing, broadcasting, or online publication) and slander (transient form, such as spoken words).

Under the Defamation Act 2013, a claimant must show that the statement has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to their reputation. For a company, serious harm means serious financial loss. This threshold was introduced to prevent trivial claims from clogging the courts.

A defendant may rely on several defences. The defence of truth (formerly justification) provides that a statement cannot be defamatory if it is substantially true. The defence of honest opinion (formerly fair comment) protects statements of opinion on a matter of public interest, provided the opinion is one that an honest person could hold based on the facts. The defence of publication on a matter of public interest provides protection where the defendant reasonably believed publishing the statement was in the public interest.

Where defamation is established, the claimant may seek damages, an injunction preventing further publication, or an order requiring the defendant to publish a summary of the court's judgment. English courts have traditionally awarded substantial damages for defamation, though the courts now take a more restrained approach.

questions.question: What is the main distinction between libel and slander?
options: Libel is more serious than slander
Libel is in permanent form; slander is in transient form
Libel requires proof of damage; slander does not
Libel is a criminal offence; slander is civil
questions.correct: Libel is in permanent form; slander is in transient form
questions.explanation: Libel involves defamatory statements in a permanent form (writing, broadcast, online). Slander refers to transient forms, primarily spoken words.

questions.question: Under the Defamation Act 2013, what must a claimant demonstrate?
options: That the statement was published internationally
That the statement caused or is likely to cause serious harm to their reputation
That the defendant intended to cause harm
That the statement was published more than once
questions.correct: That the statement caused or is likely to cause serious harm to their reputation
questions.explanation: The Defamation Act 2013 introduced a 'serious harm' threshold — a claimant must show the statement has caused or is likely to cause serious reputational harm.

questions.question: What does the defence of 'truth' provide?
options: Protection if the defendant genuinely believed the statement was true
A complete defence if the statement is substantially true
Protection only for statements made in good faith
questions.correct: A complete defence if the statement is substantially true
questions.explanation: The defence of truth (formerly justification) is a complete defence — if the defendant can prove the statement is substantially true, the claim fails entirely.

questions.question: What remedy requires the defendant to publish a correction?
options: An order to publish a summary of the court's judgment
questions.correct: An order to publish a summary of the court's judgment
questions.explanation: Under the Defamation Act 2013, courts can order a defendant to publish a summary of the judgment, effectively requiring them to publicise their defeat.

questions.question: What threshold did the Defamation Act 2013 introduce, and why?
options: A financial threshold, to ensure only wealthy claimants could sue
A 'serious harm' threshold, to prevent trivial claims from clogging the courts
An intent threshold, requiring proof of malice
A publication threshold, requiring proof of widespread publication
questions.correct: A 'serious harm' threshold, to prevent trivial claims from clogging the courts
questions.explanation: The 'serious harm' threshold was introduced to filter out minor or trivial defamation claims and ensure that only genuinely significant cases reached the courts.

collocations.sentence: The defendant relied on the defence of ___ to argue the published statement was substantially true.
The claimant sought an ___ preventing the newspaper from republishing the article.
The statement was held to ___ the claimant's reputation in the eyes of right-thinking members of society.
